claim: The study describes Nanjinganthus dendrostyla gen. et sp. nov. from the South Xiangshan Formation (Early Jurassic) of China based on observations of 264 specimens of 198 individual flowers preserved on 34 slabs.
source: Here, based on observations of 264 specimens of 198 individual flowers preserved on 34 slabs in various states and orientations, from the South Xiangshan Formation (Early Jurassic) of China, we describe a fossil flower, Nanjinganthus dendrostyla gen. et sp. nov..
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of specimens, flowers, and slabs examined, along with their geological formation and age.

claim: Nanjinganthus has an invaginated receptacle and ovarian roof that completely enclose the seeds.
source: From the evidence of the combination of an invaginated receptacle and ovarian roof, we infer that the seeds of Nanjinganthus were completely enclosed.
evidence: The manuscript describes morphological features observed in the specimens that indicate seed enclosure.

claim: Nanjinganthus is an angiosperm from the Jurassic based on its actinomorphic flower with a dendroid style, cup-form receptacle, and angiospermy.
source: Evidence of an actinomorphic flower with a dendroid style, cup-form receptacle, and angiospermy, is consistent with Nanjinganthus being a bona fide angiosperm from the Jurassic, an inference that we hope will re-invigorate research into angiosperm origins.
evidence: The authors infer angiosperm affinity based on observed morphological features and geological age.

claim: There are no reliable records of angiosperms from pre-Cretaceous rocks according to a conclusion made almost 60 years ago that was recently re-confirmed.
source: although the conclusion 'there are no reliable records of angiosperms from pre-Cretaceous rocks' made almost 60 years (Scott et al., 1960) seemed to be recently re-confirmed (Herendeen et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites two sources (Scott et al., 1960 and Herendeen et al., 2017) that support this conclusion.

claim: Some scholars have proposed that angiosperms existed before the Cretaceous.
source: Since the time of Darwin, some scholars have proposed that angiosperms existed before the Cretaceous (Smith et al., 2010; Clarke et al., 2011; Zeng et al., 2014; Buggs, 2017)
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple sources supporting pre-Cretaceous angiosperm existence.

claim: Some reports of early angiosperms like Monetianthus are based on a single specimen, which restricts further testing and confirming.
source: Some reports of early angiosperms (i.e., Monetianthus (Friis et al., 2001)) are based on a single specimen, which restricts further testing and confirming.
evidence: The manuscript cites Monetianthus as an example and explains the limitation of single-specimen studies.

claim: Nanjinganthus flowers are subtended by bracts that are fused basally.
source: Flowers subtended by bracts. Bracts fused basally.
evidence: This is stated in the generic diagnosis section based on specimen observations.

claim: Nanjinganthus flowers are pedicellate, actinomorphic, epigynous, with inferior ovary.
source: Flowers pedicellate, actinomorphic, epigynous, with inferior ovary.
evidence: This is stated in the generic diagnosis based on specimen observations.

claim: Nanjinganthus has 4-5 sepals that are rounded in shape with usually 4-6 longitudinal ribs in the center and two lateral rib-free laminar areas.
source: Sepals 4–5, rounded in shape, each with usually 4–6 longitudinal ribs in the center and two lateral rib-free laminar areas, attached to the receptacle rim with their whole bases, surrounding the petals when immature, with epidermal cells with straight cell walls.
evidence: This morphological description is based on direct observation of specimens.

claim: Nanjinganthus has 4-5 petals that are cuneate and concave with usually 5-6 longitudinal ribs in the center and two lateral rib-free laminar areas.
source: Petals 4–5, cuneate, concave, each with usually 5–6 longitudinal ribs in the center and two lateral rib-free laminar areas, with rounded tips, surrounding the gynoecium when immature, with epidermal cells with straight cell walls.
evidence: This morphological description is based on direct observation of specimens.

claim: The gynoecium of Nanjinganthus is unilocular and fully closed by a cup-form receptacle from the bottom and sides and by an integral ovarian roof from above.
source: Gynoecium in the center, unilocular, fully closed by a cup-form receptacle from the bottom as well as sides and by an integral ovarian roof from the above.
evidence: This structural description is based on specimen observations.

claim: Nanjinganthus has a dendroid-formed style centrally attached on the top of the ovarian roof.
source: Style centrally attached on the top of the ovarian roof, dendroid-formed.
evidence: This morphological feature is described based on specimen observations.

claim: Nanjinganthus contains one to three seeds inside the ovary that are elongated oval and hanged on the ovarian wall by a thin funiculus.
source: One to three seeds inside the ovary, elongated oval, hanged on the ovarian wall by a thin funiculus, with the micropyle-like depression almost opposite the chalaza.
evidence: This description is based on direct observation of seeds in specimens.

claim: The type locality of Nanjinganthus is Wugui Hill, Sheshan Town, Qixia District, Nanjing, China (N32˚08″ 19′, E118˚58″ 20′).
source: Wugui Hill, Sheshan Town, Qixia District, Nanjing, China (N32˚08″ 19′ , E118˚58″ 20′) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific geographic coordinates for the type locality.

claim: The horizon of Nanjinganthus is the South Xiangshan Formation, the Lower Jurassic.
source: The South Xiangshan Formation, the Lower Jurassic.
evidence: The manuscript states the geological formation and age.

claim: The flowers of Nanjinganthus are frequently concentrated and preserved in groups on certain bedding surfaces.
source: The flowers are frequently concentrated and preserved in groups on certain bedding surfaces (Figures 1a–g and 2a–b), although many of them are preserved as isolated individuals on other slabs.
evidence: The manuscript describes the preservation pattern and references figures showing grouped flowers.

claim: A flower bud of Nanjinganthus is preserved as a coalified compression, 6.4 mm long and 3 mm wide, with characteristic longitudinal ribs on the sepals and petals.
source: A flower bud is preserved as a coalified compression, 6.4 mm long and 3 mm wide, with characteristic longitudinal ribs on the sepals and petals (Figure 2g).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific measurements and preservation type for a flower bud specimen.

claim: Mature flowers of Nanjinganthus are 8.4–10.7 mm in length and 6.8–12.8 mm in diameter.
source: The flowers are preserved in various states (including coalification), with cup-form receptacle, epigynous with an inferior ovary, 8.4–10.7 mm in length and 6.8–12.8 mm in diameter, actinomorphic in the bottom and top views
evidence: The manuscript provides specific size measurements for mature flowers.

claim: The pedicel of Nanjinganthus is approximately 0.76 mm in diameter.
source: The pedicel is approximately 0.76 mm in diameter (Figure 6a,b).
evidence: The manuscript provides a specific measurement for the pedicel diameter.

claim: Basally fused bracts 0.7–3.7 mm long are observed at the bottom in a few flowers of Nanjinganthus.
source: Basally fused bracts 0.7–3.7 mm long are observed at the bottom in a few flowers, and a stoma is seen on a bract (Figures 4g-h, 7e,h, and 8h).
evidence: The manuscript provides measurements and references figures showing bracts.

claim: A stoma is seen on a bract of Nanjinganthus.
source: Basally fused bracts 0.7–3.7 mm long are observed at the bottom in a few flowers, and a stoma is seen on a bract (Figures 4g-h, 7e,h, and 8h).
evidence: The manuscript reports observation of a stoma on a bract specimen.

claim: The receptacle of Nanjinganthus is cup-form, 3–4.8 mm in diameter and 2–4.5 mm high, surrounded by a 0.3 mm thick wall.
source: The receptacle is cup-form, 3–4.8 mm in diameter and 2–4.5 mm high, surrounded by a 0.3 mm thick wall in the bottom and sides, and covered by an ovarian roof from the above (Figures 2h–i, 4d, 5h, 6a–b and 7a,e–f,i).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific measurements for the receptacle structure.

claim: Scales are attached on the sides of the receptacle/ovary of Nanjinganthus.
source: Scales are attached on the sides of the receptacle/ovary (Figures 3a–b, 4a,g–h, 5i and 7a,e,i).
evidence: The manuscript describes scales observed on specimens.

claim: The sepals of Nanjinganthus are 1.7–3 mm long and 2.7–4.3 mm wide.
source: The sepals are 1.7–3 mm long and 2.7–4.3 mm wide, with two lateral rib-free laminar areas and usually four longitudinal ribs in the center, and attached to the receptacle rim with their whole bases (Figures 2c-f, 3d-f, 4a,b,d-e, 5i,l, 6l, 7e,i, 9a).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific measurements for sepal dimensions.

claim: The elongated epidermal cells of Nanjinganthus sepals are 44–156 μm x 33–54 μm with straight cell walls in the middle region.
source: The elongated epidermal cells are, 44–156 μm x 33–54 μm, with straight cell walls in the middle region, while isodiametric epidermal cells 16–71 μm x 10–54 μm are seen in the lateral laminar areas of the sepals (Figures 8g, 9h-k and 10d-f).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific measurements of epidermal cell dimensions.

claim: Isodiametric epidermal cells 16–71 μm x 10–54 μm are seen in the lateral laminar areas of Nanjinganthus sepals.
source: The elongated epidermal cells are, 44–156 μm x 33–54 μm, with straight cell walls in the middle region, while isodiametric epidermal cells 16–71 μm x 10–54 μm are seen in the lateral laminar areas of the sepals (Figures 8g, 9h-k and 10d-f).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific measurements of epidermal cell dimensions.

claim: The petals of Nanjinganthus are 3.1–6.6 mm long and 1.9–5.4 mm wide, compressed to only about 11 μm thick.
source: The petals are 3.1–6.6 mm long, 1.9–5.4 mm wide, compressed to only about 11 μm thick, with two lateral rib-free laminar areas, a cuneate base, and 5–6 longitudinal ribs in the center, located inside the sepals on the rim of the receptacle (Figures 2c–f,h,j,4a,b,d,6a,f,7a,e,i,8a–f,9a–g).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific measurements for petal dimensions.

claim: The ribs on Nanjinganthus petals are approximately 0.12 mm wide and fork only basally.
source: The ribs are approximately 0.12 mm wide, forking only basally, with elongated epidermal cells with straight cell walls, 32–144 μm x 17–30 μm on the abaxial and 19–72 μm x 13–29 μm on the adaxial (Figures 8a-f, 10a-b).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific measurements for rib width and describes their branching pattern.

claim: A possibly immature stoma is seen on one of the petals of Nanjinganthus.
source: A possibly immature stoma is seen on one of the petals (Figure 10c).
evidence: The manuscript reports observation of a possible stoma on a petal.

claim: An unknown organ (possibly a staminode) is seen once on the rim of the receptacle of Nanjinganthus.
source: An unknown organ (staminode?) is seen once on the rim of the receptacle (Figure 6a,m).
evidence: The manuscript reports observation of an unidentified structure with speculative interpretation.

claim: The ovarian roof of Nanjinganthus is horizontal with smooth integral outer and inner surfaces, 0.14–0.22 mm thick.
source: The ovarian roof is horizontal, with smooth integral outer and inner surfaces, 0.14–0.22 mm thick, with a style vertically located on its center (Figures 4c, 5h, 6f and 7a–c,e–g).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific measurements and descriptions of the ovarian roof structure.

claim: The style of Nanjinganthus is 0.3–0.8 mm in diameter with lateral branches that make the width of the style 3–6 mm.
source: The style is 0.3–0.8 mm in diameter, with lateral branches that make the width of the style 3–6 mm (Figures 2h–i, 3a–b, 5i–j, 6a,c and 7a–d).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific measurements for the style dimensions.

claim: The basalmost pair of lateral branches on the style of Nanjinganthus appear oppositely arranged.
source: The basalmost pair of the lateral branches appear oppositely arranged along the style (Figures 2h and 3b) while the upper ones appear irregularly arranged (Figures 2i, 6a and 7c–d).
evidence: The manuscript describes the arrangement pattern of style branches based on specimen observations.

claim: The upper lateral branches on the style of Nanjinganthus appear irregularly arranged.
source: The basalmost pair of the lateral branches appear oppositely arranged along the style (Figures 2h and 3b) while the upper ones appear irregularly arranged (Figures 2i, 6a and 7c–d).
evidence: The manuscript describes the arrangement pattern of style branches based on specimen observations.

claim: There are longitudinal faint striations on the surface of the style of Nanjinganthus.
source: There are longitudinal faint striations on the surface of the style (Figures 3c and 5j).
evidence: The manuscript describes surface features observed on the style.

claim: There are 1.6–3.6 mm long and 1.7–2.2 mm wide round-triangular scales on the sides of the ovary of Nanjinganthus.
source: There are 1.6–3.6 mm long and 1.7–2.2 mm wide round-triangular scales on the sides of the ovary (Figures 2g, 3b, 4a,g–h and 5i).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific measurements for scale dimensions.

claim: Each ovary of Nanjinganthus contains one to three seeds that are 0.65–3 mm x 0.5–1.7 mm, elongated or oval-shaped.
source: Each ovary contains one to three seeds that are 0.65–3 mm x 0.5–1.7 mm, elongated or oval-shaped (Figures 2f, 5a,c and 6d,f–l), hanged on the inner wall of the ovary by a 0.08–0.27 mm wide funiculus (Figures 5e and 6d–e).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific measurements for seed dimensions and numbers.

claim: Seeds of Nanjinganthus are hanged on the inner wall of the ovary by a 0.08–0.27 mm wide funiculus.
source: Each ovary contains one to three seeds that are 0.65–3 mm x 0.5–1.7 mm, elongated or oval-shaped (Figures 2f, 5a,c and 6d,f–l), hanged on the inner wall of the ovary by a 0.08–0.27 mm wide funiculus (Figures 5e and 6d–e).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific measurements for the funiculus width.

claim: A micropyle-like depression 0.15 × 0.36 mm is seen on a seed of Nanjinganthus.
source: A micropyle-like depression 0.15 × 0.36 mm is seen on a seed (Figure 5a,d).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific measurements for a micropyle-like structure.

claim: A dendroid style is seen in ten flowers of Nanjinganthus across multiple specimens.
source: A dendroid style is seen in ten flowers (four in PB22224, Figures 2h and 3a–b; four in PB2222a, Figures 2i, 5f–g, 6a and 7d; one in PB22282, Figure 7a–c; one in PB22489, Figure 5i–j).
evidence: The manuscript documents the occurrence of dendroid styles across multiple specimens.

claim: The repeated occurrences of a dendroid style in specimens of Nanjinganthus underscore its truthful existence.
source: The repeated occurrences of such an unexpected feature in the specimens of Nanjinganthus underscore its truthful existence.
evidence: The authors infer the reality of the dendroid style based on its repeated observation.

claim: The dendroid-form distal portion of the gynoecium may be branched stigmas in Nanjinganthus.
source: The dendroid-form distal portion of the gynoecium may be branched stigmas in Nanjinganthus.
evidence: The authors propose a possible interpretation of the dendroid structure.

claim: It is possible that the lateral appendages on the style of Nanjinganthus are actually pollen sac complexes, as are similarly attached on the style in extant Malvaceae.
source: But it is possible that these lateral appendages on the style are actually pollen sac complexes, as are similarly attached on the style in extant Malvaceae (Judd et al., 1999).
evidence: The authors propose an alternative interpretation citing a comparison with extant plants.

claim: Meticulous fluorescence microscopic examination of the dendroid structure in Nanjinganthus found no trace of pollen grains.
source: We have performed a meticulous fluorescence microscopic examination of this structure and found no trace of pollen grains, reducing the possibility that these lateral branches are clusters of pollen sacs, which is the case seen in some angiosperms (Malvaceae).
evidence: The manuscript reports the results of microscopic examination.

claim: The absence of pollen grains in the dendroid structure reduces the possibility that the lateral branches are clusters of pollen sacs.
source: We have performed a meticulous fluorescence microscopic examination of this structure and found no trace of pollen grains, reducing the possibility that these lateral branches are clusters of pollen sacs, which is the case seen in some angiosperms (Malvaceae).
evidence: The authors infer from the absence of pollen grains that the structure is unlikely to be pollen sacs.

claim: A branched distal projection is apparently lacking in all known gymnosperms.
source: A branched distal projection is apparently lacking in all known gymnosperms, but it has been seen some derived angiosperms, such as Passifloraceae, Poaceae and Euphorbiaceae (Heywood, 1978).
evidence: The authors make a comparative statement about gymnosperms and cite examples from angiosperms.

claim: A branched distal projection has been seen in some derived angiosperms, such as Passifloraceae, Poaceae and Euphorbiaceae.
source: A branched distal projection is apparently lacking in all known gymnosperms, but it has been seen some derived angiosperms, such as Passifloraceae, Poaceae and Euphorbiaceae (Heywood, 1978).
evidence: The manuscript cites examples of angiosperms with branched projections.

claim: One advantage of a branched style is the increased receptive area, which is conducive to anemophilous pollination.
source: One of the advantages of a branched style is the increased receptive area, which is conducive to anemophilous pollination.
evidence: The authors propose a functional interpretation of the branched style.

claim: The occurrence of a branched style in Nanjinganthus might suggest that Nanjinganthus had yet not established a close cooperation with animals (insects).
source: The occurrence of such feature in Nanjinganthus might suggest that Nanjinganthus had yet not established a close cooperation with animals (insects).
evidence: The authors speculate about the pollination biology of Nanjinganthus based on its morphology.

claim: A branched style is not seen among extant basal angiosperms sensu APG.
source: However, it is noteworthy that this feature is not seen among extant basal angiosperms sensu APG (Chase et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference about basal angiosperms and notes the absence of this feature.

claim: No trace of carpels typical of Magnoliales has been seen in Nanjinganthus.
source: We have not seen any trace of the carpels typical of Magnoliales, which were previously believed by some to represent ancestral angiosperms.
evidence: The authors report the absence of a specific morphological feature.

claim: The seeds are physically enclosed by the cup-form receptacle and ovarian roof in Nanjinganthus.
source: The seeds are physically enclosed by the cup-form receptacle and ovarian roof in Nanjinganthus.
evidence: The manuscript describes the structural enclosure of seeds.

claim: The enclosure of seeds by the cup-form receptacle and ovarian roof constitutes the foundation for interpreting Nanjinganthus as an angiosperm.
source: This constitutes the foundation based on which we justify our interpretation of Nanjinganthus as an angiosperm.
evidence: The authors explain their reasoning for classifying Nanjinganthus as an angiosperm.

claim: The lack of carpel typical of Magnoliales cannot prevent Nanjinganthus from being an angiosperm as many angiosperms are actually 'acarpellate'.
source: The lack of carpel typical of Magnoliales cannot prevent Nanjinganthus from being an angiosperm as many angiosperms are actually 'acarpellate' (Heads, 1984; Sattler and Lacroix, 1988).
evidence: The authors cite references supporting the existence of acarpellate angiosperms.

claim: In some basal angiosperms such as Nymphaea (Nymphaeales) and derived angiosperms such as Cactaceae, the ovary is inferior and the seeds are attached to the ovarian walls.
source: It is noteworthy that, at least in some of basal angiosperms such as Nymphaea (Nymphaeales) (Taylor, 1991; Taylor, 1996) and derived angiosperms such as Cactaceae (Boke, 1964), the ovary is inferior and the seeds are attached to the ovarian walls.
evidence: The manuscript cites references describing similar features in other angiosperms.

claim: The enclosure of seeds in Nanjinganthus is fulfilled by the cup-form receptacle from the bottom and the ovarian roof from above.
source: The enclosure of the seeds is fulfilled by the cup-form receptacle from the bottom and the structure here-called 'ovarian roof' (preserved complete in Figures 4c, 5h and 7e–g, but partially preserved in Figures 2f, 5c and 6f,j,l) from the above.
evidence: The manuscript describes how seed enclosure is achieved structurally.

claim: The intact ovarian roof is clearly seen in side view and surface view in Nanjinganthus specimens.
source: The intact ovarian roof is clearly seen in the side view (Figure 7f–g) and in surface view (Figures 4c and 5h), in the latter case the seeds inside ovary are fully eclipsed by the ovarian roof.
evidence: The manuscript describes observations of the ovarian roof in different views.

claim: The varying preservation status of the ovarian roof suggests that it has fully enclosed the ovules in its original status, and the loss of ovarian roof and exposure of seeds are artifacts due to preservation.
source: This series of varying preservation status of ovarian roof suggests that the ovarian roof has fully enclosed the ovules in its original status, and the loss of ovarian roof and exposure of seeds are artifacts due to preservation.
evidence: The authors infer the original condition from the preservation patterns observed.

claim: The length about 1 mm suggests that the structures in Nanjinganthus are most likely to be seeds rather than ovules.
source: We cannot recognize the maturity of the ovules/seeds in Nanjinganthus, the length about 1 mm suggests that they are most likely to be seeds rather than ovules, therefore we prefer to use the term 'seed' rather 'ovule' throughout this paper.
evidence: The authors infer seed identity based on size.

claim: The number of seeds in Nanjinganthus is variable and may be one, two, or even three.
source: The number of seeds in Nanjinganthus is variable. According to our observation, it may be one (not shown), two (Figure 6f–i), or even three (Figure 6j–k).
evidence: The manuscript reports observed variation in seed number.

claim: Caytoniales can be easily distinguished from Nanjinganthus by its cupule with an adaxial basal opening, bilateral reproductive organs, and lack of both a dendroid style and foliar appendages in its reproductive organs.
source: Caytonia can be easily distinguished from Nanjinganthus by its cupule with an adaxial basal opening, bilateral reproductive organs, and lack of both a dendroid style and foliar appendages in its reproductive organs.
evidence: The authors compare morphological features to distinguish Nanjinganthus from Caytoniales.

claim: Corystospermales can be easily distinguished from Nanjinganthus by their cupule which has an abaxial basal opening, bilateral reproductive organs, and the lack of both a dendroid style and foliar appendages in the reproductive organs.
source: Corystospermales can be easily distinguished from Nanjinganthus by their cupule which has an abaxial basal opening, bilateral reproductive organs, and the lack of both a dendroid style and foliar appendages in the reproductive organs.
evidence: The authors compare morphological features to distinguish Nanjinganthus from Corystospermales.

claim: Ginkgoales can be easily distinguished from Nanjinganthus by their clustered naked seeds and lack of a dendroid style in the reproductive organs.
source: Ginkgoales can be easily distinguished from Nanjinganthus by their clustered naked seeds, and lack of a dendroid style in the reproductive organs.
evidence: The authors compare morphological features to distinguish Nanjinganthus from Ginkgoales.

claim: Czekanowskiales can be easily distinguished from Nanjinganthus by their bivalvate cupules, bilateral reproductive organs, and lack of both a dendroid style and foliar appendages in the reproductive organs.
source: Czekanowskiales can be easily distinguished from Nanjinganthus by their bivalvate cupules, bilateral reproductive organs, and lack of both a dendroid style and foliar appendages in the reproductive organs.
evidence: The authors compare morphological features to distinguish Nanjinganthus from Czekanowskiales.

claim: Irania's female and male parts are not concentrated on the same axis and do not constitute a flower-like structure.
source: Its female and male parts are not concentrated on the same axis, and do not constitute a flower-like structure, and it is unknown whether the seeds are enclosed.
evidence: The manuscript describes characteristics of Irania for comparison.

claim: Pentoxylales can be easily distinguished from Nanjinganthus by their cones which are devoid of any foliar appendages and the lack of a dendroid style.
source: Pentoxylales can be easily distinguished from Nanjinganthus by their cones which are devoid of any foliar appendages and the lack of a dendroid style.
evidence: The authors compare morphological features to distinguish Nanjinganthus from Pentoxylales.

claim: Bennettitales can be easily distinguished from Nanjinganthus by their cones with ovules bearing micropylar tubes and lack of a dendroid style.
source: Bennettitales can be easily distinguished from Nanjinganthus by their cones with ovules bearing micropylar tubes, and lack of a dendroid style (Taylor et al., 2009).
evidence: The authors compare morphological features to distinguish Nanjinganthus from Bennettitales, citing a reference.

claim: Gnetales can be easily distinguished from Nanjinganthus by their cones with ovules with micropylar tubes and lack of a dendroid style.
source: Like Bennettitales, Gnetales can be easily distinguished from Nanjinganthus by their cones with ovules with micropylar tubes and lack of a dendroid style.
evidence: The authors compare morphological features to distinguish Nanjinganthus from Gnetales.

claim: The cup-form receptacle with seeds inside plus the lack of pollen grains in the distal dendroid part distinguish Nanjinganthus from all male cones of conifers.
source: But the cup-form receptacle with seeds inside plus the lack of pollen grains in the distal dendroid part distinguish Nanjinganthus from all these male cones.
evidence: The authors identify distinguishing features between Nanjinganthus and conifer male cones.

claim: In coniferous cones, cone axes penetrate the cones from the bottom to the tip, which is different from Nanjinganthus in which the pedicel stops at the bottom of the ovary and the style starts above the ovarian roof.
source: As in female cones, these male cones also have cone axes penetrating the cones from the bottom to the tip and thus are different from Nanjinganthus in which the pedicel stops at the bottom of the organ (ovary) (Figure 6b) and the style starts above the ovarian roof (Figure 4c, 5h, 6a-c, 7a-c).
evidence: The authors compare structural differences between Nanjinganthus and conifer cones.

claim: None of the known gymnosperms, fossil or extant, are comparable to Nanjinganthus.
source: From the above comparison, we infer that none of the known gymnosperms, fossil or extant, are comparable to Nanjinganthus.
evidence: The authors conclude from their comparative analysis that Nanjinganthus is distinct from gymnosperms.

claim: The enclosed seeds distinguish Nanjinganthus from gymnosperms, which are not supposed to enclose their ovules in such a way.
source: The enclosed seeds distinguish Nanjinganthus from gymnosperms, which are not supposed to enclose their ovules in such a way (Table 1).
evidence: The authors identify seed enclosure as a key distinguishing feature from gymnosperms.

claim: The cup-form receptacle, inferior ovary, and dendroid style distinguish Nanjinganthus from all Jurassic angiosperm peers including Schmeissneria, Xingxueanthus, Juraherba, and Euanthus.
source: The cup-form receptacle, inferior ovary, and dendroid style distinguish Nanjinganthus from all these Jurassic peers, and justify Nanjinganthus as a new genus of angiosperm.
evidence: The authors compare Nanjinganthus with other Jurassic angiosperms and identify distinguishing features.

claim: Angio-ovuly before pollination is the key character that distinguishes an angiosperm from other seed plants.
source: Although multiple characters have been suggested to identify fossil angiosperms (Herendeen et al., 2017), angio-ovuly before pollination is the key character that distinguishes an angiosperm from other seed plants (Tomlinson and Takaso, 2002; Wang, 2010a; Wang, 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple references supporting this criterion for angiosperm identification.

claim: The integral ovarian roof of Nanjinganthus has no opening.
source: The integral ovarian roof of Nanjinganthus has no opening (Figures 4c and 5h).
evidence: The manuscript describes the structural integrity of the ovarian roof based on specimen observations.

claim: The ovarian roof can block sediment from entering the ovarian locule after burial.
source: After burial, this ovarian roof can block the sediment from entering the ovarian locule (Figure 7e–g).
evidence: The manuscript describes taphonomic evidence supporting the integrity of the ovarian roof.

claim: The space inside the ovary remaining free of sediment suggests a full enclosure of the ovules/seeds, securing an angiospermous affinity for Nanjinganthus.
source: That this space remained free of sediment suggests a full enclosure of the ovules/seeds, securing an angiospermous affinity for Nanjinganthus.
evidence: The authors infer seed enclosure from taphonomic evidence.

claim: The radial arrangement of two whorls of foliar parts (sepals and petals) in Nanjinganthus is very similar to those of flowers in extant angiosperms.
source: The radial arrangement of two whorls of foliar parts (sepals and petals) in Nanjinganthus is very similar to those of flowers in extant angiosperms (Figures 1a–b and 2a–f)
evidence: The manuscript compares the arrangement pattern in Nanjinganthus with extant angiosperms.

claim: Nanjinganthus satisfies all thirteen definitions of flowers advanced by various authors.
source: Furthermore, Nanjinganthus satisfies all thirteen definitions of flowers advanced by various authors (Bateman et al., 2006).
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference and claims Nanjinganthus meets all flower definitions.

claim: Common features of model ancestral angiosperms include apocarpy, superior ovary, and lack of obvious style.
source: The common features of these model plants include apocarpy, superior ovary, lack of obvious style, etc.
evidence: The manuscript describes features of hypothetical ancestral angiosperms based on existing models.

claim: Features of model ancestral angiosperms (apocarpy, superior ovary, lack of obvious style) are rarely seen in Nanjinganthus or other early angiosperms.
source: However, these features are rarely seen in Nanjinganthus or other early angiosperms (Wang et al., 2007; Wang and Zheng, 2009; Wang, 2010b; Wang, 2018; Han et al., 2013; Han et al., 2016; Han et al., 2017; Liu and Wang, 2016; Liu and Wang, 2017; Liu et al., 2018; Liu and Wang, 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple references about early angiosperms that lack these features.

claim: An inferior ovary is clearly seen in Nanjinganthus and quite many Early Cretaceous flowers.
source: Instead, an inferior ovary, a feature unexpected by, at least, most theories of angiosperm evolution, is clearly seen in Nanjinganthus and quite many Early Cretaceous flowers (Friis, 1984; Friis, 1990; Friis et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript cites references documenting inferior ovaries in early angiosperms.

claim: The discrepancy between fossil observation and theories suggests either that inferences based on living plants have limited capability of 'predicting' past history, or that angiosperms originated polyphyletically, or that angiosperms have a history that dates back to a time much earlier than the Cretaceous, or a combination of these.
source: This discrepancy between fossil observation and theories suggests EITHER that inferences based on living plants have limited capability of 'predicting' past history, OR that angiosperms originated polyphyletically, each lineage has followed a different evolution route, and Nanjinganthus represents one of the many, OR that angiosperms have a history that dates back to a time much earlier than the Cretaceous, and Nanjinganthus is one of the many derived from such assumed ancestor, OR a combination of these.
evidence: The authors propose multiple alternative interpretations of the implications of their findings.

claim: The currently dominant theories of angiosperm evolution apparently need to be reassessed.
source: Whatever the implications are, the currently dominant theories of angiosperm evolution apparently need to be reassessed.
evidence: The authors conclude that existing theories require reevaluation based on their findings.

claim: Most Nanjinganthus specimens are concentrated on certain bedding surfaces, and over 50 individual flowers are preserved on a single slab.
source: Most Nanjinganthus specimens are concentrated on certain bedding surfaces, and over 50 individual flowers are preserved on a single slab (Figures 1a–g and 2a–b)
evidence: The manuscript describes the preservation pattern of specimens.

claim: The concentration of Nanjinganthus specimens suggests that Nanjinganthus may have flourished and dominated a particular niche.
source: suggesting that Nanjinganthus may have flourished and dominated a particular niche, although Nanjinganthus played only an inferior role in the broader Jurassic ecosystem.
evidence: The authors infer ecological dominance in a specific niche from preservation patterns.

claim: The concentrated preservation of delicate flowers is more likely a result of autochthonous preservation, suggesting a habitat very close to water for Nanjinganthus.
source: The concentrated preservation of delicate flowers is more likely a result of autochthonous preservation, suggesting a habitat very close to water for Nanjinganthus.
evidence: The authors infer habitat from taphonomic patterns.

claim: Various studies on the South Xiangshan Formation and palynological analysis as well as U/Pb dating suggest a latest Early Jurassic age for Nanjinganthus.
source: Various studies (including palaeobotany) on the South Xiangshan Formation in the last century (Hsieh, 1928; Li et al., 1935; Sze and Chow, 1962; Zhou and Li, 1980; Cao, 1982; Cao, 1998; Cao, 2000; Wang et al., 1982; Huang, 1983; Huang, 1988; Ju, 1987) and our palynological analysis as well as U/Pb dating (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Supplementary file 2; Santos et al., 2018) suggest a latest Early Jurassic age for Nanjinganthus.
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple studies and presents dating evidence for the age determination.

claim: Nanjinganthus with over 200 specimens is consistent with a pre-Cretaceous origin of angiosperms.
source: Together with the 'unexpectedly' great diversity of angiosperms in the Early Cretaceous (Sun et al., 1998; Sun et al., 2001; Sun et al., 2002; Leng and Friis, 2003; Leng and Friis, 2006; Ji et al., 2004; Wang and Zheng, 2009; Wang and Zheng, 2012; Wang and Han, 2011; Han et al., 2013; Han et al., 2017; Wang, 2015; Liu et al., 2010a), pollen grains indistinguishable from angiosperms in the Triassic (Hochuli and Feist-Burkhardt, 2004; Hochuli and Feist-Burkhardt, 2013), a bisexual flower from the Jurassic (Liu and Wang, 2016), and an herbaceous angiosperm from the Middle Jurassic (Han et al., 2016), the unexpectedly early age of Poaceae (Prasad et al., 2011; Wu et al., 2018) and Solanaceae (Wilf et al., 2017), Nanjinganthus with over 200 specimens is consistent with a pre-Cretaceous origin of angiosperms.
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple lines of evidence from various sources supporting pre-Cretaceous angiosperm origin.

claim: Nanjinganthus demonstrates a certain resemblance to Pentapetalae sensu Judd et al., 2016.
source: The systematic position of Nanjinganthus is now apparently open to further investigation, although it demonstrates a certain resemblance to Pentapetalae sensu (Judd et al., 2016).
evidence: The authors note a resemblance to a specific angiosperm group while acknowledging uncertainty.

claim: It is premature to determine the phylogenetic position of Nanjinganthus before more information of contemporaneous peers is available.
source: It is premature to determine its phylogenetic position before more information of contemporaneous peers is available, although we welcome all phylogeneticists to evaluate Nanjinganthus in their own ways and perspectives.
evidence: The authors acknowledge limitations in determining phylogenetic position.

claim: The Xiangshan Group was initially called the 'Nanking Sandstein' and was put in the Upper Carboniferous by Richthofen in 1912.
source: Initially, what is now known as the Xiangshan Group was called the 'Nanking Sandstein' that was put in the Upper Carboniferous by Richthofen (1912).
evidence: The manuscript cites historical geological nomenclature.

claim: Liu and Chao (1924) thought that the Nanking Sandstein belonged to the Jurassic and renamed it the 'Tsung Shan Formation'.
source: Liu and Chao (1924) thought that the Nanking Sandstein belonged to the Jurassic and renamed it the 'Tsung Shan Formation'.
evidence: The manuscript cites historical geological nomenclature changes.

claim: Li et al. (1935) changed the 'Tsungshan Formation' to 'Xiangshan Layers' and regarded its age as being the Early Jurassic.
source: They also changed the 'Tsungshan Formation' to 'Xiangshan Layers', and regarded its age as being the Early Jurassic.
evidence: The manuscript cites historical geological nomenclature and age determination.

claim: Sze and Chow (1962) used the term 'Xiangshan Group' for the previous 'Xiangshan Layers', and this has been the convention followed ever since.
source: Sze and Chow (1962) used the term 'Xiangshan Group' for the previous 'Xiangshan Layers', and this has been the convention followed ever since.
evidence: The manuscript cites the establishment of current geological nomenclature.

claim: Ju (1987) divided the Xiangshan Group into a lower South Xiangshan Formation and an upper North Xiangshan Formation.
source: Ju (1987) divided the Xiangshan Group into a lower South Xiangshan Formation and an upper North Xiangshan Formation, respectively.
evidence: The manuscript cites the subdivision of the geological formation.

claim: The standard section of the South Xiangshan Formation is 394 meters thick in South Xiangshan in Nanjing and has yielded abundant fossil plants.
source: The standard section of the lower part of the Xiangshan Group (the South Xiangshan Formation, the Lower Jurassic) is 394 meters thick in South Xiangshan in Nanjing, and has yielded abundant fossil plants.
evidence: The manuscript provides geological information about the formation thickness and fossil content.

claim: Cao (1982) thought that the age of the South Xiangshan Formation could not be later than the Early Jurassic.
source: Based on fossil plants, Cao (1982) thought that the age of the South Xiangshan Formation could not be later than the Early Jurassic
evidence: The manuscript cites age determination based on fossil plants.

claim: Cao (1982) regarded the age of the lower part of Xiangshan Group (=South Xiangshan Formation) as the middle-late Early Jurassic.
source: Cao (1982) regarded the age of the lower part of Xiangshan Group (=South Xiangshan Formation) as the middle-late Early Jurassic.
evidence: The manuscript cites a specific age determination for the formation.

claim: The South Xiangshan Formation includes sandstones, siltstones, shales, carbonaceous shales, and coal seams.
source: The formation includes sandstones, siltstones, shales, carbonaceous shales, and coal seams.
evidence: The manuscript describes the lithology of the formation.

claim: According to various authors, the Xiangshan Group includes at least 46 genera of plants.
source: According to Cao (1982), Cao (1998), Cao (2000), Wang et al. (1982), and Ju (1987), the Xiangshan Group includes at least 46 genera of plants
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple sources documenting plant diversity.

claim: Cycadophytes (34%) dominate the Xiangshan flora, and ferns are the second most dominant group (20%).
source: Cycadophytes (34%) dominate the flora, and ferns are the second most dominant group (20%), among which Dipteridaceae play an important role.
evidence: The manuscript cites the composition of the flora.

claim: Preliminary analysis of the strata yielding Nanjinganthus has recognized abundant palynomorphs.
source: Preliminary analysis of the strata yielding Nanjinganthus has recognized abundant palynomorphs.
evidence: The manuscript reports results of palynological analysis.

claim: The palynological assemblage suggests a latest Early Jurassic age for Nanjinganthus.
source: This palynological assemblage suggests a latest Early Jurassic age for Nanjinganthus.
evidence: The authors infer age from palynological data.

claim: There was no previous isotopic age for the Xiangshan Group.
source: There was no previous isotopic age for the Xiangshan Group.
evidence: The manuscript states the absence of prior isotopic dating.

claim: The zircon grains from layers above the fossiliferous layers appeared to be reworked, with ages ranging from 2738 Ma to 207 Ma.
source: The zircon grains appeared to be reworked (Supplementary file 2), with ages ranging from 2738 Ma to 207 Ma (67 zircon grains with the concordance >90% from 168 zircon grains), and 207 Ma (two zircon grains) is the youngest age (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports isotopic dating results.

claim: 207 Ma is the youngest zircon age and represents the upper limit age of Nanjinganthus (the Late Triassic).
source: So the upper limit age of Nanjinganthus is 207 Ma (the Late Triassic).
evidence: The authors interpret the youngest zircon age as the upper age limit.

claim: Most of the zircon grains were of magmatic origin with internal oscillation belts and high Th/U values, implying a granitic provenance.
source: Most of the zircon grains were of magmatic origin with internal oscillation belts and high Th/U values, implying a granitic provenance.
evidence: The manuscript reports geochemical characteristics of zircons and infers their origin.

claim: The age of Nanjinganthus falls in the scope ranging from 174 to 207 Ma and is closer to 174 Ma (the latest Early Jurassic).
source: Taking all dating information into consideration, we think that the age of Nanjinganthus falls in the scope ranging from 174 to 207 Ma and is closer to 174 Ma (the latest Early Jurassic).
evidence: The authors synthesize multiple lines of dating evidence to determine age range.

claim: The conclusion on absolute age of Nanjinganthus is in agreement with megafossil biostratigraphical analysis.
source: Such a conclusion on absolute age of Nanjinganthus is in agreement with megafossil biostratigraphical analysis (Cao, 1982; Huang, 1983; Huang, 1988; Ju, 1987)
evidence: The manuscript cites biostratigraphic studies that support the age determination.

claim: The fossils studied were collected from an outcrop of the South Xiangshan Formation at a quarry owned by the Xiaoyetian Cement Company Ltd. in the northeastern suburb of Nanjing, Jiangsu, China.
source: The fossils studied here were collected from an outcrop of the South Xiangshan Formation at a quarry owned by the Xiaoyetian Cement Company Ltd. in the northeastern suburb of Nanjing, Jiangsu, China (N32˚08′ 19′′, E118˚58′ 20′′) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific collection locality information.

claim: The fossil plants closely associated with Nanjinganthus constitute a flora dominated by Dipteridaceae (Clathropteris) and various cycadophytes (mainly Nilssonia, Ptilophyllum, and Pterophyllum).
source: our collection from the local outcrop indicates that the fossil plants closely associated with Nanjinganthus constitute a flora dominated by Dipteridaceae (Clathropteris) and various cycadophytes (mainly Nilssonia, Ptilophyllum, and Pterophyllum), which is consistent with previous works.
evidence: The manuscript describes the associated flora based on collection data.
